note_tweet.text:
What if we could teach dexterous robots through natural human demonstrations—with human data only?

Introducing TouchBridge: transferring contact-rich skills from human hands to robot hands through touch. 🖐️🤖

📄 arXiv: https://t.co/zuu7twaFdx
🌐 Website & demos: https://t.co/4kXC0swMSI

Across 4 real-world tasks, TouchBridge achieves 72.5% average success using human data only, compared with 77.5% using the same number of teleoperated robot demonstrations. Human demonstration collection is 7.0× faster.

The key: capture how fingers contact an object, then preserve those contacts when transferring the demonstration to a different hand.

No object meshes, object-pose estimates, or physics simulation are needed for retargeting.

From turning book pages to screwing in a light bulb—here’s how it works. 🧵👇

note_tweet.text:
"Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems" — new paper (arXiv, Nov 3). https://t.co/N4CkEdTUIq

Most AI products pick one strong model and send it everything. The pitch for routing is that you shouldn't: for each request, pick whichever model or policy is best for that input, and you get better answers, or the same answers for less money.

A team from NUS's HPC-AI Lab, Inf Rec's Cardinal AI Lab, UC Berkeley and HKUST tested that idea far beyond chatbots. They ran 452 candidate configurations on the same inputs across 25 benchmarks: text and image questions, image, video and speech generation, coding and workplace agents, and robot manipulation. That is 374,401 scored runs. Then they trained small routers (a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B) to pick a candidate per input.

What they found:

1. The ceiling is real. If you could pick the best candidate for every single input, you'd beat the best fixed model per benchmark by 5.4 points on 19,814 test inputs (82.60 vs 87.98). The gap is tiny for speech generation (0.7) and huge for video generation and robots (18–19 points), where no single candidate dominates.

2. Most of that gain hides inside task types. Picking the best model per capability type, even in hindsight, closes only 8% of the gap. The winner changes input by input, and part of it is plain noise: on AA-LCR, where every question was answered three times, the oracle's 2.4-point edge vanished once each model was scored by its average.

3. Learned routers barely beat a fixed model on quality. One router over 16 benchmarks scored 79.98 against 79.68 for the best fixed candidate, with the oracle at 84.80. On two image benchmarks, none of 124 router configurations beat the fixed generator significantly. On robots, a router reading three camera frames got 71.6% success vs 70.5% for the best single policy, with 24% less policy time.

4. The real win is cost. Against always calling the strongest model, routing raised efficiency 8.82× on average across four testbeds. On CodeRouterBench (9,999 coding tasks, reference Claude Opus 4.6), the router fitted for zero quality loss never called Opus at all and reached 25.5× its efficiency at a 0.44-point loss. Always calling the cheapest model, Qwen3-Max, got 20.1× but lost 4.2 points.

Where it breaks: a router fitted for "no quality loss" on training data often doesn't keep that promise. Refitted on half the data, the zero-loss floor held on test in only 12.5% of 200 splits. Their fix is a statistical certification step on held-out inputs, which held in all 200 at a median 19.4×.

Two more details matter if you build these systems. Retrying with a second model after a failure works worse than you'd think: across 42 model pairs, the second model succeeded about half as often (median ratio 0.49), because failures leave the harder tasks. And the baseline setup can flip the result: a fixed baseline that dropped Opus 5.5 for missing 11 of 1,122 scores turned a router's 0.4-point deficit into a 2.4-point gain.

Who should care: anyone paying for frontier API calls on mixed traffic. The message is not "routing makes you smarter" but "routing makes you cheaper, if you compare on the same inputs and check the quality floor on data the router never saw."
